skills.name: Control systems, virtual reality and augmented reality

note.text:
A computer control system uses sensors to monitor conditions, a processor to compare readings with a set value, and actuators to make changes; the cycle repeats (feedback).
Examples: automatic doors, traffic lights, air conditioning and thermostats, greenhouse watering, automatic street lights.
Virtual reality (VR): a fully computer-generated world that the user enters with a headset; used for games, training pilots and surgeons, virtual tours.
Augmented reality (AR): computer information placed on top of the real world, usually through a phone camera or smart glasses; used for navigation arrows, furniture apps, educational models, games.

sections.heading: Computers in control
Virtual reality (VR)
sections.text:
VR replaces what you see and hear with a computer-made world. You wear a headset with a screen for each eye and often hold controllers.
It is used for games, training pilots, drivers and surgeons safely, and visiting places you cannot travel to. Some people feel dizzy, and headsets can be expensive.

sections.heading: Augmented reality (AR)
sections.text:
AR keeps the real world in view and adds computer information on top, usually through a phone camera or smart glasses.
Examples: navigation arrows on the street, apps that show how a sofa would look in your room, {3}-D models of the heart on your desk, and games that place characters in your surroundings.
Remember: VR = a new world; AR = extra information on the real world.

key_words.meaning: a system that senses, decides and acts automatically
measuring the result of an action and using it to decide the next action
computer information added to the real world

examples: AR: navigation arrows on the phone camera

mistake.wrong: AR and VR are the same
mistake.right: VR replaces the real world; AR adds to it
mistake.why: In AR you still see your real surroundings.

worked_example.problem: Describe how an air-conditioning control system keeps a room at {set} °C.
steps: A temperature sensor measures the room temperature.
The processor compares it with the set value of {set} °C.
If it is higher, the processor switches the cooling on (actuator); if lower, it switches it off.
The sensor keeps measuring, so the loop repeats (feedback).
worked_example.answer: Sensor → compare with {set} °C → switch cooling on or off → repeat

cards.idea: Control systems: sensor → processor (compare) → actuator, repeated.
example: A street light switches on when the light sensor reads 'dark'.

cards.idea: VR replaces the real world with a computer-made one.
example: A headset shows a {3}-D virtual classroom.

cards.idea: AR adds computer information to the real world.
example: A phone shows arrows on the street for directions.

pick.q: Plants in a greenhouse need water when the soil is dry.
pick.r: a moisture sensor that switches on a water pump
w: a light sensor that switches on a fan
a sound sensor that opens a door
a motion sensor that switches on a radio
pick.y: Measure soil moisture; act with a pump.

pick.q: Street lights in Limbe should come on at dusk.
pick.r: a light sensor that switches on the lamps when it gets dark
e: Temperature does not show dusk reliably.
pick.y: Light level decides when to switch.

pick.q: A room must not get warmer than 26 °C.
pick.r: a temperature sensor controlling a fan or air conditioner
w: a light sensor controlling the lamps
a motion sensor controlling the door
a moisture sensor controlling a pump
e: Doors do not control heat directly.

pick.q: In an automatic door, what is the sensor?
pick.r: a motion (infrared) sensor above the door
w: the motor that opens the door

pick.q: What does the processor do in a control system?
pick.r: Compares sensor readings with set values and decides what to do

pick.q: Why is a control system called a feedback loop?
pick.r: The result of each action is measured again by the sensor

pick.q: A trainee pilot wears a headset and flies in a fully computer-made sky.
e: AR keeps the real world in view.
No sensors control a device here.

pick.q: A phone camera shows the street with arrows drawn on it to guide you.
e: The real street is still visible.
Information is added to the real view.
pick.y: Information on top of the real world: AR.

pick.q: An app places a 3-D model of a heart on your desk through the phone camera.
e: Your real desk is still seen.
It is not fake news; it is a learning model.
pick.y: A virtual object added to the real scene.

pick.q: Why is VR useful for training surgeons?
pick.r: They can practise many times without risk to real patients
w: It is cheaper than any book
e: That is not the main reason.

pick.q: Which is a disadvantage of VR headsets?
pick.r: Some users feel dizzy and they can be expensive
pick.y: Motion sickness and cost are common problems.

pick.q: Why are computer control systems used for traffic lights?
pick.r: They react to traffic and work all day without a person
w: They need a police officer at each light
e: They manage traffic, not stop it.
pick.y: Sensors can detect queues and change timings.
